Good Wednesday morning. This is Andrew McDonald in Birmingham.

AND NOW, THE END IS NEAR: Four long days in Birmingham reach their climax this morning with Kemi Badenoch’s speech to the Conservative Party conference. The Tory leader will take the stage at 11.15 a.m. with the same aim she has had all week: to promote her lengthy pamphlet vision in spoken word form … energize the small but upbeat band of members in the hall … and convince far more casual viewers of the lunchtime news that they should sell shares in Reform UK and buy Kemi, two years after they sent her party into the wilderness at the last election. The only remaining question is whether the rabbit in her hat will match the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty, before we all do a mass Griffith exit.

I’ll state my case, of which I’m certain: Badenoch will deliver some fighting talk to the foot soldiers who have been in an optimistic mood, despite the polls (and it’s worth noting on that front that the Tories sit nine points behind Labour). She’ll say Andy Burnham and his bold new promises have created a “fight that we have not seen in this country for more than half a century.” It’s true that Westminster is in a place it hasn’t been in for a long time: a Labour and Tory leader with eye-catching rhetoric and a stark contrast in ideology who are both popular with their own MPs. She’ll even say it is a “battle for the soul of this nation.” One Reform wag pointed out sounds pretty similar to the famous Joe Biden speech from 2022.

I’ve loved, I’ve laughed, I’ve cried: The other big difference between Badenoch and Burnham last week is that she’ll go on the attack. We’ve already seen policies like the £100,000 childcare threshold that appeal to core Tory support and lean into an ideological battle about helping the better off. She’ll also accuse the PM of delivering “dangerous” ideas on TikTok, tax rises instead of tax cuts, a bigger state and seeing “no need to fix the public finances,” according to pre-briefed words from CCHQ — which are largely focused on her belief the country is “running out of money.”

**A message from Lloyds Banking Group: Financial empowerment is taking shape differently across the UK. Nationally nearly nine in ten (88%) digital tool users engage with their finances digitally at least once a week. But what are they using those tools for? And what do those choices reveal about the financial priorities of people locally? Lives Empowered. A Nation Empowered.**

Helpfully for her …  Burnham’s occasional economic adviser Andy Haldane told CNBC on Tuesday that Britain is “skating on pretty thin ice in fiscal terms” and that the PM should appease the markets by showing the country is “able and willing to take the knife to public spending.” If he doesn’t, says Haldane, the PM will remain “in hock to the bond market.” That sounds like the type of thing Badenoch would throw in Burnham’s face if we were getting the usual PMQs knockabout today. One for her deputy Alex Burghart on the morning broadcast round.

THE BIT WE’RE ALL WAITING FOR: What Badenoch says about inheritance tax, on which Tories widely expect an announcement. Her most senior aides were tight-lipped last night on what exactly is coming this morning.

Tea leaf reading: There were persistent rumors and some reporting before this conference that the Tories were looking to scrap that tax altogether.
